This is a cheap, immediately-visible AAA opportunity: tone-driven accent color, icon, and a brief impact flash/shake on 'danger'/'boss' cues would make reinforcement warnings and boss reveals read like a AAA mission banner the moment they appear, at near-zero risk because the data already exists and is plumbed through. (Styling lives in src/styles/game.css, outside scope, but the data contract that enables it is here.)
evidence: cue() factory (lines 5-6) stores tone; danger cues at lines 32-34/38/68/73/100/105/132/137, boss at 40/75, success at 27/34/41 etc. main.js 34361 `root.dataset.tone=cue.tone||'story';` is the only consumer.
fix: In src/styles/game.css add `#story-cue[data-tone="danger"]`, `[data-tone="boss"]`, `[data-tone="success"]` accent rules (left-border color, tag color) plus a one-shot keyframe flash on those tones; reuse the existing storyCueIn keyframe. No JS change needed — the tone is already on the element.
risk: Low. CSS-only; falls back to current look if a tone is missing. Confirm contrast/a11y.

title: Compiled custom map lighting is a single hemi + one key, much flatter than campaign
description: Compiled custom maps get only a HemisphereLight(intensity 0.42) and one DirectionalLight key (0.92) with no fill/rim light and no CSM cascades, versus the campaign's managed room lights + CSM. Even with the loaded HDR environment providing IBL, the lack of any fill light and (currently) any working shadow means surfaces read flat and the scene feels noticeably less 'AAA' than the campaign the instant you enter a custom map. Pairs with the shadow-frustum finding above.
evidence: `const hemi = new THREE.HemisphereLight(0xaac4dd, 0x17130f, 0.42); ... const key = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffd49a, 0.92); ... key.castShadow=false;` — only two lights, no fill/rim.
fix: Add a low-intensity cool fill DirectionalLight (e.g. `new THREE.DirectionalLight(0x66ccff, 0.3)` from the opposite side, castShadow=false) and push to localObjects so cleanup removes it — mirroring the editor viewport which already adds a fill light (levelEditor.js:695). Cheap and immediately visible. Combine with the shadow-frustum fix for the biggest jump.
risk: Low. Additive light; must push to localObjects so disposeRoot/cleanup removes it (avoid leaking lights across map loads). No save-compat impact.

title: Animated CRT monitor material exists but only 2-3 wall monitors use it
description: monitorScreenM (line 3508) is a live emissive-map CRT screen driven by _drawMonitorCanvas every 3rd frame (43945) — a genuinely AAA animated-screen asset. But buildLevel only places 2 generic wallMonitor calls (plus one for bn>=2), and all the per-building screens (B5 vital monitors line 4090, B6 ticket/map screens, B8 terminal monitors 4294/4845, helm displays 4183) use flat static MeshBasicMaterial cyan/black quads instead of the animated monitorScreenM. The expensive animated-screen feature is under-used, so most 'screens' in the game are dead flat color while the system to make them live already runs each frame.
evidence: wallMonitor uses monitorScreenM, but e.g. B8 terminal: `const monM=new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0x40c8ff});` (line 4294); B5 vitals: `new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0x040608})` (4090); helm: `new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0x40c8ff})` (4183).
fix: Swap a handful of the most player-facing static screen MeshBasicMaterials to share monitorScreenM (the emissiveMap texture is shared so cost is one canvas redraw, already happening). At minimum: B8 terminal monitors (4294), B5 reception monitor (4708), helm display panels (4183). Reuse the single monitorScreenM instance (do NOT clone — it shares _monitorTex). Instant 'screens are alive' upgrade with near-zero added cost.
risk: monitorScreenM is MeshPhongMaterial; replacing MeshBasicMaterial planes changes lighting response (screens become slightly lit). Verify they still read as bright (emissiveIntensity 1.10 keeps them glowing). Shared material so no extra disposal. Don't apply to planes that need exact alignment as bezels.

title: Faked god-ray cones only render on low/medium; high/ultra get nothing unless Phase2 volumetrics shipped
description: useConeGodrays is set to `!cinemaRayQ` where cinemaRayQ is true for high/ultra. The comment says high+ should instead get the Phase 2 volumetric post pass. If a player runs on high/ultra but Phase 2 volumetrics is disabled/absent (SETTINGS.phase2Volumetrics not true), the result is NO light-shaft volumetrics at all under the ceiling lamps — high/ultra can look flatter than medium for that one effect. Low/medium get the cheap cone shafts; high/ultra fall through to (possibly absent) post FX.
evidence: let useConeGodrays=!cinemaRayQ; try{ if(SETTINGS.phase2Volumetrics===false)useConeGodrays=false; }catch(_){}  — for high/ultra cinemaRayQ is true so useConeGodrays starts false; only the explicit ===false re-confirms off, never turns the cones back on.
fix: If the Phase 2 volumetric post pass is not actually active, keep the cheap cones on for high/ultra too: `let useConeGodrays=!cinemaRayQ || !(SETTINGS && SETTINGS.phase2Volumetrics===true);` so high/ultra without the post pass still get shafts. Verify the post-pass path actually runs before relying on it (check _renderStack for a volumetric pass) to avoid double shafts.
risk: Could double-render shafts if Phase 2 volumetrics IS active — gate carefully on the same flag the post pass reads. The cone material opacity is .012 so even if both ran the artifact is faint. Validate visually per quality tier.

title: Cathedral choir-loft candles are bare emissive cylinders with no pool/glow lamp
description: B10 choir loft places four candle meshes as plain MeshBasicMaterial cylinders (color 0xffe8b0) with no accompanying fakeCeilingLamps pool entry and no flicker. Other set-piece lights in the function (chandelier 3853, disco 3906, fountain 3990, fireplace 4002) all call _aaPushFakePoolLamp so the lighting controller tints nearby surfaces. The cathedral's signature votive candles contribute zero light interaction and don't flicker — they look like glowing toothpicks rather than candlelight in the level whose whole identity is 'votive candle pools in deep gothic shadow' (lightProfile comment line 3112).
evidence: const candle=new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.06,0.08,0.30,8),new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0xffe8b0})); candle.position.set(cx,chY+0.40,-22); scene.add(candle);ob.push(candle); — no _aaPushFakePoolLamp, no dynProps flicker.
fix: For each candle add a small additive glow sphere + a fake pool lamp: `_aaPushFakePoolLamp(fakeCeilingLamps,cx,chY+0.55,-22,0xffd090,1.2,{candle:true});` and optionally register a subtle flicker (reuse the L.userData.flicker path or a dynProps 'fire'-style scale jitter on a small flame plane). High atmospheric payoff for the cathedral.
risk: Adds 4 fake lamps to B10 (fake lamps are budget-free meshes, not PointLights). Keep additive glow opacity low to avoid bloom blowout. No state impact.

title: Explosion sparks are low-poly SphereGeometry blobs instead of the textured additive spark quads used by the rest of the VFX
description: spawnExplosionFx scatters 18 sparks as MeshBasicMaterial spheres (SphereGeometry(.06,5,4)). They read as faceted orange dots rather than streaky embers. Elsewhere the game uses billboarded textured spark quads (e.g. line 29934 sparksAtlasQuad with _softRadialTex, billboardRoll, drag/gravity) which look far more 'AAA'. Swapping the explosion sparks to the same soft-radial additive billboards (with motion blur from billboardRollSpeed + drag) would noticeably upgrade the grenade blast that the player sees constantly.
evidence: const s=new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(.06,5,4),m); ... G.trails.push({mesh:s,mat:m,vel:v,timer:.7,maxTime:.7,isParticle:true});
fix: Replace the sphere spark with a small PlaneGeometry using _softRadialTex (additive), set faceCameraBillboard:true, billboardRoll/billboardRollSpeed, drag:.88 and gravity, mirroring the muzzle/impact spark pattern at lines 29934/24285. Keep count/timer the same to preserve perf budget.
risk: Low. Same trail category (isParticle) and lifetime; uses an already-loaded shared texture. Verify _trailBudget particle cap isn't exceeded (count unchanged at 18).

title: Enemy muzzle flash is a flat on/off pop — add a 2-3 frame additive decay + brief warm light for punch
description: The enemy muzzle flash sets opacity (0.92/0.88/0.70 * scale) to a single value, then a 55ms timeout snaps it to 0 (see related finding). There is no decay curve, so enemy gunfire reads as a flat sprite blink rather than a hot flash. The infrastructure is already in place (H/V/D planes, per-shot color by shot type, scale jitter) — adding a quick per-frame opacity falloff and a sub-frame scale punch is a cheap, immediately visible upgrade to enemy gunfights, which the player sees constantly.
evidence: line 12902: `e.muzzleFlashH.material.opacity=0.92*_sc;e.muzzleFlashH.scale.setScalar(_sc);` — set once, never animated; hidden by the 55ms setTimeout with no interpolation.
fix: When converting to the frame-loop fade (see enemy-muzzleflash-settimeout-after-remove), ease opacity = base * (remaining/55)^1.4 each frame, and start scale at ~1.25*_sc easing down to _sc, so the flash blooms then collapses. Optionally, for the player's current target only (single enemy), add a very short-lived cheap warm flicker on the enemy's already-present accent/visor emissive (multiply by ~1.6 for one frame) to sell the shot without adding a PointLight (respecting the no-PointLight perf note at line 12890).
risk: Low/visual only. Keep the additive blend and respect _trailBudget/_additiveVfxTierMul tier scaling already used for the smoke puff at 12906 so low-end tiers stay cheap.

title: _flashScreenColor uses mix-blend-mode:screen at z-index:14 — likely under the HUD and dependent on backdrop; opacity .55 is harsh
description: _flashScreenColor appends a full-screen div with mix-blend-mode:screen, opacity .55, z-index:14. mix-blend-mode:screen blends with whatever is BEHIND it in the same stacking context; a fixed overlay at z-index 14 may sit below HUD layers and its 'screen' blend can be effectively invisible over dark scenes or wash out over bright ones. If cinematicKillEnhanced is wired, this is the on-screen feedback, so it should be tuned to AAA standards.
evidence: f.style.cssText='position:fixed;inset:0;pointer-events:none;z-index:14;mix-blend-mode:screen;background:#'+hex...+';opacity:.55';
fix: Use a brief radial-vignette flash (background:radial-gradient(circle, transparent 35%, color 120%)) or a quick opacity .55->0 with mix-blend-mode:plus-lighter and a z-index just under the crosshair but above the world canvas, and shorten/keyframe the alpha (e.g. .45 -> 0 over 220ms) for a snappier hit feel. Keep pointer-events:none.
risk: Cosmetic only; ensure z-index doesn't cover interactive HUD. No save/perf impact.

title: Dropkick launch has shake + gun dip but no camera FOV punch — cheap way to make the lunge read as a committed AAA move
description: _startDropkick applies shakeY/shakeX and a small gunGrp dip, but does not punch FOV. A brief FOV widen on launch (then ease back) is the single cheapest cue that makes a flying-kick lunge feel powerful (Sifu/Doom-style). The codebase already animates camera params per-frame, so a transient _dropkickLaunchSurge is already set (27442) and could drive an FOV add.
evidence: 27451-27454: PP.shakeY-=...; PP.shakeX+=...; gunGrp.position.y-=.038; gunGrp.position.z+=.042;  — no FOV/exposure punch. _dropkickLaunchSurge is set (27442) but only feeds body motion.
fix: On launch set a transient fov-kick pulse (e.g. P._fovKick=Math.max(P._fovKick||0, P.dropkickTargeted?6:4)) and decay it in the camera update where FOV is composed; on contact (_checkDropkickHit, 27659) add a sharper inward FOV snap. Verify the project's existing FOV-composition site before adding a new field (search for camera.fov assignment).
risk: Low-medium. Must hook into the existing FOV composition rather than writing camera.fov directly, or it will fight ADS/sprint FOV. Confirm the single FOV writer first.

title: Muzzle flash light is modest (intensity ~3-4) — a brighter, slightly longer flash reads far more AAA
description: The per-shot muzzle dynamic light peaks at only 3.0-4.0 intensity with 0.55 plane opacity for 52ms. There is already a dynamic point light + flash plane + AAA world spill (spawnAaaMuzzleWorldSpill) + ring + smoke, so the plumbing is solid — but the punch is conservative. A modest bump to peak intensity and a touch more opacity, combined with the game-time decay fix above, makes every shot pop and light up nearby walls/enemies the instant you fire, which is one of the cheapest, most immediately visible AAA upgrades.
evidence: `light.intensity=(3.0+(Math.random()*1.0))*suppressedMul; mat.opacity=0.55*suppressedMul;`
fix: Raise the peak (and let randomness vary it more), e.g. `light.intensity=(5.5+Math.random()*2.0)*suppressedMul;` and `mat.opacity=0.72*suppressedMul;`, ideally paired with the frame-loop decay so it sustains a hair longer in real frames. Tune against renderer exposure/tone-mapping so it flashes without clipping the whole frame.
risk: Low; purely visual tuning. If the renderer uses strong bloom/tone-mapping, validate it doesn't over-bloom indoors. Easy to revert.

title: Objective ticker HUD is a flat box — cheap polish opportunity
description: The objective ticker (B05/B07/B10) is created as a plain dark box with a thin progress bar. _refreshObjectiveHud (32044) already computes rich feel values (urgency/holding/cadence/anticipation) and even applies a subtle translateY + boxShadow, but the base element has no entrance animation, no icon glow, and the fill bar transition is a flat 0.1s linear. For a story objective this reads unfinished next to the rest of the polished HUD.
evidence: 32098 inline cssText is a static box; fill 32107 `transition:width .10s linear`; the feel-driven styling at 32057-32065 is good but the static base undercuts it.
fix: Add a CSS entrance (slide+fade-in) on creation, an animated accent glow keyed off feel.objectiveCadence (already computed), and an ease on the fill (cubic-bezier). All driven by values already in _refreshObjectiveHud — near-zero risk, immediately visible during the three story buildings.
risk: Very low. Pure CSS/inline-style polish on an existing element.

title: Global screen-shake (PP.shakeX/Y) is applied to camera only as a tiny POSITIONAL offset (x0.012 / x0.008) and never as rotation — explosions/hits barely move the view
description: PP.shakeX/PP.shakeY accumulate sizable impulses across the game (explosions push 1.6/1.2 at 23176-23177, near-miss/recoil push 0.06-0.3 at 13356-13378, melee 0.13-0.20 at 14301-14302). But the ONLY place they feed the view is the camera POSITION at 42826 (`PP.shakeX*.012`) and 42827 (`PP.shakeY*.008`). A 0.3 impulse therefore yields ~0.0024-0.0036m of camera translation — visually negligible — and there is no angular (camera.rotation) shake from PP at all. The big, screen-selling 'kick' AAA shooters use is angular. This is a cheap, high-visibility upgrade: route a small fraction of PP.shake into camera.rotation. (Verified PP.shake is read nowhere else; decay at 44524-44525 with shakeDecay=11 is well-behaved, so increasing the camera mapping is safe.)
evidence: 42826 `...+PP.shakeX*.012+adsBX+...` 42827 `EYE+P._camBobY+P.jumpH+PP.shakeY*.008-P.landKick+...`. Inputs e.g. 23176 `PP.shakeX+=(Math.random()-.5)*1.6;` 13357 `PP.shakeY-=(hit?.315:.135)*s;`. No `PP.shake*` appears in any camera.rotation expression (camera.rotation lines 42952-42955 reference _pa0/recoil/feel pulses only).
fix: After the camera.rotation.z assignment block (around 42955), add a small angular term, e.g. `camera.rotation.x+=PP.shakeY*0.020; camera.rotation.z+=PP.shakeX*0.014;` (tune to taste; multipliers chosen so a 0.3 impulse gives ~0.4deg pitch). Keep the existing positional terms. This is purely additive and decays with the existing shakeDecay. Optionally clamp with an SETTINGS.screenShake scale if one exists.
risk: Adding rotation shake can cause motion sickness if overdone and could fight the recoil angular kick — start conservative (0.01-0.02). Gate behind any existing SETTINGS.screenShake/reducedMotion flag if present. No save/perf concern; one extra add per frame.

title: Sharpening is applied twice: inside the color-grade pass and again by the dedicated sharpen pass
description: The color-grade shader applies an unsharp-mask term (`col = mix(col, col + (col - blur), sharpen)`, sharpen ~0.034 high) AND the pipeline adds a separate makePostSharpenPass ShaderPass (strength up to 0.34) later in the chain. Both run when post is enabled, so edges are sharpened twice, which can cause ring/halo artifacts on high-contrast edges and wastes a full-screen pass. configure() already halves grade sharpen when LUT is heavy (line 1004) but never accounts for the dedicated sharpen pass.
evidence:
// grade shader: col = mix(col, col + (col - blur), sharpen);
// plus: sharpenRuntime = makePostSharpenPass(THREE, 0.34); passes.sharpen = new ShaderPass(sharpenRuntime.material);
fix: Pick one sharpener: either set the grade pass's sharpen uniform to 0 when passes.sharpen is enabled (in configure(), guard grade.sharpen by `passes.sharpen && passes.sharpen.enabled ? 0 : value`), or skip adding the dedicated sharpen pass and rely on the grade pass. Reduces a full-screen draw and prevents over-sharpen ringing.
risk: Minor look change (slightly softer edges); could be perceived as less crisp. No build/probe impact.

title: Slide leg material opacity is driven by slide amount, not by the visibility blend (no fade on enter/exit)
description: updateSlideLegs computes a smoothed visibility `vis` (P._slideLegVis) and shows the group when vis>.025, but the per-part opacity write at the end is `m.material.opacity=.92+amt*.08`, which depends only on `amt` (slide amount), never on `vis`. So while the body-presence rig fades opacity with vis (`.30+vis*.62`) and the dropkick rig fades with `show`, the slide legs pop to ~0.92+ opacity the instant vis crosses the 0.025 threshold. The exit is partly masked because the group also slides down/back via `exitSweep`, but on entry — especially the post-slide-to-ADS clear path — the legs can flash in at near-full opacity for a frame or two rather than easing in.
evidence: Line 17489 `const vis=THREE.MathUtils.clamp(P._slideLegVis||0,0,1);` then line 17490 `slideLegsGrp.visible=vis>.025;` but lines 17527-17532: `for(const m of _SLIDE_BODY_PARTS){ if(m.material&&'opacity' in m.material){ m.material.transparent=true; m.material.opacity=.92+amt*.08; } }` — no `vis` factor.
fix: Multiply the slide opacity by the visibility blend, mirroring body presence: `m.material.opacity=(.92+amt*.08)*THREE.MathUtils.clamp(vis,0,1);` (or fade only near the edges to keep the skid mostly solid: `*THREE.MathUtils.smoothstep(vis,.025,.30)`).
risk: Pure visual; very low risk. Keep transparent=true (already set). The body-presence probe asserts its own opacity; slide legs have no equivalent assertion, so unlikely to break a probe. Confirm no perceived flicker if vis hovers near the threshold.

title: Additive cyan shin-stripe shares the global body-presence opacity, blowing out at full presence
description: _setBodyPresenceOpacity applies one opacity value (capped at .96) to EVERY material in _BODY_PRESENCE_MATERIALS, including _bodyAccentM, a MeshBasicMaterial with AdditiveBlending used for the shin stripes (shin_stripe parts). At full presence the additive stripe is pushed to ~0.96 opacity additively over the dark legs, which reads as an overly hot cyan bar rather than a subtle tech accent. Solid pant/armor materials want high opacity; an additive accent generally wants a much lower, separately-tuned alpha.
evidence: Line 17557 `const _bodyAccentM=_cloneBodyPresenceMat(new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({color:0x72d7ff,...blending:THREE.AdditiveBlending}));` is pushed into _BODY_PRESENCE_MATERIALS. Line 17618-17620: `for(const m of _BODY_PRESENCE_MATERIALS){ if(m&&Math.abs((m.opacity||0)-o)>.004)m.opacity=o; }` applies the same `o` to all, including the additive accent.
fix: Exclude the accent from the bulk setter and scale it separately, e.g. keep a reference and set `_bodyAccentM.opacity=Math.min(.55,o*.55)` after the loop, or store accent materials in a separate list with their own multiplier. This makes the stripe glow read as a tasteful edge highlight instead of a blown-out bar.
risk: Visual only; low risk. Verify body-presence-locomotion probe doesn't assert _BODY_PRESENCE_MATERIALS[0]-style opacity equality across all materials (snapshot reads _BODY_PRESENCE_MATERIALS[0], which is _bodyPantM, so safe).

title: All authored PBR map sets are network-loaded eagerly at module init (65 requests) regardless of whether the current level uses them
description: The loop over AA_AUTHORED_MATERIALS (13 material families x 5 map types = 65 textures, lines 1930-1940) fires _aaLoadTex() unconditionally at module load, kicking off 65 HTTP requests for /assets/materials/<name>/<name>-<map>.<ext> before any level is built. Each has an onError that only console.warns (line 1899), so missing sets degrade gracefully, but on first paint this competes for bandwidth/decode with the assets actually needed by building 1 and can delay the first interactive frame. Combined with the ~20 procedural CanvasTexture IIFEs (each rasterizing 256-512px canvases with thousands of fillRect calls, e.g. _wallTex 14000 dots, _carpetTex 22000 dots, _subwayConcreteTex 10000 dots) all evaluated synchronously at module init, this is a measurable boot-time stall.
evidence: for(const [name,opt] of Object.entries(AA_AUTHORED_MATERIALS)){ ... _aaAuthoredTextures[key]=_aaLoadTex(`/assets/materials/${name}/${name}-${m.suffix}.${ext}`, ...); } // runs at module top-level, all 13 families
fix: Defer authored-texture loading to first use per building (lazy-load when buildLevel(bn) requests a family), or at minimum gate the 65 requests behind requestIdleCallback so building-1 assets win the network. The heavy procedural canvas IIFEs could likewise be wrapped in lazy getters so only the textures a level uses are rasterized.
risk: Low-medium: lazy loading must preserve the synchronous fallback shape that AA_MATERIALS/_cloneConcreteFloorMaps expect (they read _aaAuthoredTextures[key] and check .isTexture). Keep the eager-allocated empty Texture objects so existing references stay valid; just defer the .load() call.

title: Grenade multi-kill spawns N overlapping money popups at the same screen anchor and N stacked money SFX in one frame
description: explodeGrenade can kill several enemies in a single blast; each kill calls awardKillMoney, which appends a moneyPopup div (all positioned identically at right:34px) and fires sfxMoney() (two oscillators each). On a 4-5 kill frag, several '+$xx' labels overlay each other at the same anchor (looks like one number) and 8-10 oscillators start simultaneously, producing a loud clipped money chime. awardKillMoney also calls hudUpdate() once per kill (cheap due to HUD cache, but redundant).
evidence: if(killed){ ... awardKillMoney(e,false); ... }  // awardKillMoney: moneyPopup(total,...); sfxMoney(); hudUpdate(); called per enemy in the radius loop
fix: Accumulate grenade kill money in the loop and emit a single consolidated moneyPopup/sfxMoney after the loop (e.g. tally `grenadeMoney` and `grenadeKills`, then one `moneyPopup(grenadeMoney, kills>1?('x'+kills):'') + sfxMoney() + hudUpdate()`). Or stagger popup vertical offset by kill index. Low priority polish.
risk: Very low. Audio/visual polish only. Ensure single hudUpdate still reflects final money.

title: Slash FX canvas sized in CSS px (no devicePixelRatio), so slash arcs render soft/blurry on HiDPI displays
description: spawnSlashFx sets the melee canvas backing-store to CSS pixels: `W=cv.width=V.w,H=cv.height=V.h` where V comes from _viewportCssPixels() (CSS px). On a 2x Retina display the WebGL canvas runs at up to 2x (renderer.setPixelRatio(min(dpr,2)) line 14729) but the slash overlay is drawn at 1x and stretched by CSS, so the otherwise crisp blood-splatter lines and slash arcs look soft compared to the sharp 3D scene behind them. A cheap sharpness/AAA uplift for melee feedback.
evidence:
14314: const V=_viewportCssPixels(),W=cv.width=V.w,H=cv.height=V.h;
14316: const cxp=W*.5,cyp=H*.52;
fix: Scale the backing store by DPR: `const dpr=Math.min(devicePixelRatio||1,2); const W=cv.width=Math.round(V.w*dpr),H=cv.height=Math.round(V.h*dpr);` then `ctx.scale(dpr,dpr)` (or multiply all coordinate constants by dpr) and keep cv CSS size at V.w/V.h. Center math should use CSS-space (V.w*.5) after ctx.scale(dpr,dpr).
risk: Low; slightly more fill cost for the brief slash draw. Ensure ctx transforms are reset (ctx.save/restore already wraps the draw). No save/probe impact.

title: Muzzle ring/corona quality is good; no change needed (clean region note)
description: addMuzzleRing already uses additive shockwave ring + atlas-sliced corona with toneMapped:false and grow/roll animation, and spawnEnemyHitPulse layers ring+core+slash+shards. This region is visually well developed; no surgical AAA win found here beyond the projectile tracer fix above. Recorded as a clean-region note to document coverage, not an issue.
evidence: addMuzzleRing: "toneMapped:false", "growRate:24", atlas corona via _sliceAtlasCell; spawnEnemyHitPulse adds core (line 24077), slashes (24096), shards (24118) with billboard + velocity.
fix: No change. If a single cheap win is desired, the highest-impact one in scope is projectile-tracer-no-length-scale.
risk: None.

title: Dropkick feet fade loop permanently forces shared materials transparent
description: The fade loop iterates _DROP_FEET_PARTS and sets `m.material.transparent=true; m.material.opacity=fade`. The boot/body materials (_dropBootM, _dropPantM, _dropArmorM, etc.) are shared across many meshes, so each is set repeatedly to the same value (harmless) but is left `transparent=true` forever, pushing fully-opaque feet into the transparent render queue (extra sorting / no early-z) every frame the rig is visible. Also, since materials are shared, opacity is effectively driven by the last mesh processed (all equal here, so visually fine).
evidence: for(const m of _DROP_FEET_PARTS){ if(m.material&&'opacity' in m.material){ m.material.transparent=true; m.material.opacity=fade; } }
fix: Set `m.material.transparent = (fade < 0.999)` so fully-opaque feet stay in the opaque queue, or fade the group via a single shared alpha and reset transparent=false when fade>=1. Tiny perf-only change; the rig is only visible during the brief kick window so impact is low.
risk: Toggling transparent flips needsUpdate; do it only on threshold crossing to avoid per-frame shader recompiles. Visual result unchanged.

title: World-space muzzle spill PointLights are added to scene with no count cap and bypass the AA pointlight budget
description: spawnAaaMuzzleWorldSpill pushes a fresh THREE.PointLight into the scene per shot (life ~0.055-0.09s). _muzzleSpills is uncapped and these lights carry no aaPointLightRole tag, so they are invisible to the carefully-managed AA_POINTLIGHT_WORLD_BUDGETED accounting in main.js. At very high fire rates (SMG/automatic) several can coexist for a frame or two, transiently spiking the active dynamic-light count above the GPU budget the rest of the lighting system tries to hold (3 managed room lights, etc.), risking shader recompile/cull hitches. Disposal is otherwise correct (tickAaaMuzzleWorldSpills removes + disposes on expiry).
evidence: aaaPresence.js L20-28: const L=new THREE.PointLight(...); scene.add(L); _muzzleSpills.push(L); — no length cap; no _tagAaPointLight; main.js light budget (e.g. updateManagedLights cap=3) does not see these.
fix: Cap _muzzleSpills (e.g. if length>=3, recycle the oldest: remove+dispose then reuse) and/or pass a tagging callback so the spill light is counted as a temp role. Cheapest: in spawnAaaMuzzleWorldSpill, if _muzzleSpills.length>=3 immediately dispose the oldest before pushing.
risk: Low. Short-lived lights; the visible flash is preserved (cap of ~3 is more than enough since each lasts <0.1s). No save/gameplay impact.

title: _syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime runs twice every frame on the authored-M4 path
description: Inside the single animation loop, _tickAuthoredM4Viewmodel(dt) (called at line 41582) invokes _syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime(now) at line 19415, and then the holo block calls _syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime(now*1000) again at line 44499. Both run in the same frame when the authored M4 hands are active. The function does heavy per-call work: facePanelToPlayer() builds quaternions via getWorldQuaternion + makeBasis for 6 panels, stabilizeReloadReadout() and syncReloadProjectionBeam() each do worldToLocal/localToWorld round-trips, plus updateMatrixWorld(true) on camera/nodes. All of this executes twice per frame. The deploy-clip toggles are idempotent (guarded by _authoredWristDeployState), so there is no logic corruption — purely wasted matrix math.
evidence: Line 19415: `_alignAuthoredHandsToM4Sockets(); _syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime(now);` (inside _tickAuthoredM4Viewmodel). Line 44499: `const _authoredHoloActive=_syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime(now*1000);` — both in the same setAnimationLoop body.
fix: Pick one call site. Either remove the call at line 19415 (let the dedicated holo block at 44499 own wristband sync) or remove line 44499's sync and reuse the result computed in _tickAuthoredM4Viewmodel (cache the boolean on a frame-scoped var / state object). Cheapest: delete the `_syncAuthoredWristbandRuntime(now)` at 19415 and have _tickAuthoredM4Viewmodel return nothing wristband-related; the 44499 call already feeds _authoredHoloActive and runs after holo deploy values are advanced.
risk: Removing the 19415 call slightly changes ordering: the 19415 call runs BEFORE reloadHoloDeployed/wristDeployed are damped this frame (those advance in the 44380-44432 block), so it actually syncs stale deploy values; the 44499 call syncs fresh values. Removing 19415 is therefore both faster and more correct, but verify hologram-* static probes stay green since they assert sync behavior.

title: _tryMove scans the full walls array linearly for broken-window vault detection even when a spatial index exists
description: Collision in _tryMove uses the spatial wall index (lines 10392-10420) for O(cell) checks, but the immediately following broken-window detection (lines 10447-10449) does a full linear pass over `walls` for every non-drone enemy on every move call (called from _moveWithVelocity each tick, plus unstick/separation passes). On large levels (B01 ~178-280 walls) this is a per-enemy-per-frame O(N) scan whose result is almost always null (few/zero broken windows).
fix: Maintain a small G.levelData.brokenWindows array (push on window-break, remove on level reset) and iterate only that, or query the same wall index cell as the collision check above and test only its walls for .broken. Either reduces the scan from ~N walls to ~0-a-few.
risk: Low. Must keep the broken-window list in sync with window shatter/reset events; if a level rebuilds windows the list must be cleared. Behavior identical if the list is correct.

title: Per-frame THREE.Vector3 allocation in enemy nav-follow hot path (one alloc per navigating enemy per frame)
description: In the nav-path follow branch, line 10657 allocates `new THREE.Vector3(wp.x,0,wp.z)` and passes it to _moveTo every frame for every enemy that is following a nav path. With multiple active enemies this is a steady stream of short-lived Vector3s feeding GC pressure during firefights (the worst time for a GC hitch). The non-path fallback at 10650 reuses `tgt`, so only this branch allocates.
evidence: L10656-10657: const wp=this.navPath[Math.min(this.navPathIdx,this.navPath.length-1)]; this._moveTo(new THREE.Vector3(wp.x,0,wp.z),dt,walls);
fix: Add a per-enemy scratch vector (e.g. this._navTgt = this._navTgt || new THREE.Vector3()) and do `this._navTgt.set(wp.x,0,wp.z); this._moveTo(this._navTgt,dt,walls);`. Confirm _moveTo does not retain the reference across frames (it reads, doesn't store).
risk: Very low if _moveTo only reads the target. If _moveTo stores the vector, use a module-level scratch instead. Behavior identical.
